activities.anchor: A weed is simply a plant growing where it competes
activities.caption: file each weed control by its layer
activities.name: agWeedLayerBuckets

config.prompt: The lesson stacks weed controls in layers. File each tactic:

items.label: rotations that swap crop architecture and planting dates
narrower rows so the canopy closes sooner
stale seedbeds — germinate the flush, kill it, then drill

config.why: Weeds are a resource-competition problem, so control is about timing and canopy rather than eradication — and tillage is effective but energy-costly and soil-damaging in excess.

activities.anchor: roughly the first third of the crop's life
activities.caption: locate the critical period on the crop's calendar
activities.name: agCriticalPeriodPlace

config.prompt: In most row crops, weed competition costs yield inside one window. Place the marker where that window begins — as a fraction of the crop's life.
config.why: Crops tolerate early weeds up to a competitive-balance date, and again after canopy closure. The window between — roughly the first third of the crop's life — is where competition costs yield.

activities.anchor: Below a density where damage cost exceeds control cost
activities.caption: true or false — the economics that ends the calendar
activities.name: agThresholdJudge

statements.s: Spraying below the economic threshold loses money twice.
statements.why: You pay the chemical spend, and you kill beneficial insects that were doing free work.

statements.s: A bug seen means a bug spray is needed.
statements.why: Most insects in a field are neutral or beneficial. Blanket spraying kills the pest's enemies faster than the pest.

statements.s: Calendar spraying can produce resurgent pest outbreaks and secondary pests.
statements.why: Spider mites formerly suppressed by their own enemies explode after broad-spectrum sprays.

statements.s: Scouting turns pest management from a calendar into a measurement discipline.
statements.why: Counts per plant or per sweep net, compared to threshold tables, are what make the decision a measurement.

activities.caption: bet on the cautionary tale first
activities.name: agToadPredict

config.q: The cane toad was released in Australia in 1935 as a biological control agent. What happened?
choices: It controlled the pest and became a model programme copied worldwide
It ate everything except the target pest and became an invasive catastrophe
It died out within a season and left no trace
It controlled the pest but had to be re-released every year
config.why: It ate everything except the pest. Modern classical programmes run through quarantine screening and host-specificity testing for exactly this reason — a serious release is the opposite of hope.

activities.caption: pair each vertex of the triangle with its cheapest attack
activities.name: agTriangleMatch

config.prompt: Plant disease needs three vertices together. Match each vertex to the control that attacks it:

pairs.right: resistant varieties plus certified disease-free seed and tubers
spacing, pruning and drip irrigation instead of overhead wetting
fungicides plus cleaning boots and machinery between fields

config.why: Pathogens travel on the farmer — hygiene rules matter more than any product. And most protectant fungicides work only before infection: they stop spores germinating and do nothing for tissue already colonised.

activities.caption: guess the scale of the resistance record
activities.name: agResistanceEstimate

config.prompt: Roughly how many arthropod species resist at least one insecticide?
config.why: More than 500 arthropod species resist at least one insecticide, and herbicide-resistant weeds number in the hundreds of species-site combinations. Every repeated control selects for survivors.
config.context: A club of 500-plus species, and Darwin collects his royalty on every overused mode of action.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this resistance plan
activities.name: agResistanceSpot

config.prompt: A student writes a resistance-management plan. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Resistance management is population genetics at field scale.
Rotate modes of action — the IRAC and FRAC numbering systems exist so labels can say Group 4 this year, Group 9 next.
Mix products with different modes, and keep refuge blocks whose susceptible pests dilute resistance genes.
When resistance appears, spray more often and use half doses to wear the survivors down.
Integrate cultural, mechanical and chemical controls, and when you do spray, dose fully.
config.correction: When resistance appears, never under-dose — under-dosing selects hardest of all; dose fully and rotate modes of action instead.
config.why: Under-dosing is the worst move available: the partially-resistant heterozygotes survive a half dose and breed. Raising frequency or halving the dose only strengthens the selection.

activities.anchor: Scouting finds an average of 12 aphids per
activities.caption: make the call with a count in hand
activities.name: agAphidBranch

config.root: Scouting finds an average of 12 aphids per wheat tiller in late spring, with ladybird larvae and parasitoids visibly working the field. The advisory threshold sits around 5–10 per tiller when predators are scarce, but rises when beneficial activity is visible.

start.text: The count is above the bare threshold, but the field's own defence is employed and doing part of the work.

choices.label: Spray a broad-spectrum pyrethroid now — 12 is over the number
choices.feedback: The spray costs about 20 €/ha and deletes the parasitoids that would have carried suppression into the next generation.

choices.label: Hold, and re-scout in a few days
choices.feedback: Thresholds rise when predators are present — a count is only half the decision.

broad.text: Aphids rebound into a thinner enemy landscape, and the spray bill is paid for a suppression you already had for free.

hold.text: Two weeks later the population has plateaued — the predators caught up — and no spray is ever spent.

config.why: Same field, same pest, opposite decisions: the difference is a count, a weather note, and a look for ladybird larvae. Reverse the case — 20 aphids per tiller, predators absent, cold weather — and a single selective spray (pirimicarb spares ladybirds; a pyrethroid kills both) is the right move.

activities.caption: rank the converters on the feed-to-gain ladder
activities.name: agFcrOrder

config.prompt: Feed conversion ratio is kilograms of feed per kilogram of live-weight gain. Order these from BEST converter to WORST:
items: Chickens — about 1.7 kg feed per kg gain
Pigs — about 3 kg feed per kg gain
Beef cattle — about 6–10 kg feed per kg gain
config.why: The trophic lesson's ten-percent law compounded through another level. Ruminants' offsetting superpower is rumen fermentation: microbes digest cellulose, converting grass and crop residues that humans and pigs cannot eat.

activities.anchor: which is why precision feeding pays
activities.caption: guess the forgotten nutrient
activities.name: agWaterEstimate

config.prompt: How many litres of water does a dairy cow drink in a day?
config.why: 60–100 litres a day, so about 80 is the working figure. Water is the first nutrient and the most forgotten: intake limits milk before any other factor.
config.context: Roughly a bathtub's worth, every day, before a single kilogram of feed is counted.

activities.caption: drag between two very different comfort zones
activities.name: agComfortCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider: two animals, opposite ends of the thermometer.

before.label: lactating dairy cow
before.text: Thermal comfort roughly 5–20 °C. She is a walking furnace — her problem is shedding heat, which is why ventilation, not heating, is the core dairy engineering. Outside the zone she eats less and drops milk yield.

after.label: newborn piglet
after.text: Needs 30–34 °C at birth. Far outside that range a piglet huddles and chills — which is why farrowing rooms run heat lamps over cold-snouted mothers, heating the small animal rather than the whole room.

config.why: Housing exists to control what weather does to productivity and health. Outside the thermal comfort zone, feed intake shifts to thermoregulation instead of production.

activities.anchor: is the first line: quarantine for
activities.caption: file each herd measure by the job it does
activities.name: agBiosecurityBuckets

config.prompt: Livestock health is managed as a herd problem. File each measure:

items.label: boot dips, dedicated clothing, rodent and wild-bird control
all-in/all-out batching with disinfection between groups
count eggs, dose by weight, leave refugia untreated

config.why: Biosecurity is the disease lesson's chain-of-transmission logic applied to gates and lorries. The parasite rules are the IPM lesson's refuge strategy in a paddock — deliberately untreated animals so susceptible genes dilute resistance.

activities.anchor: Selective breeding is husbandry's slow machine
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this breeding history
activities.name: agBreedingSpot

config.prompt: A student summarises the breeding record. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Selective breeding is husbandry's slow machine, and it compounds.
Broiler chickens reached about 2.5 kg in 12 weeks in the 1950s; the modern bird does it in under 6 weeks.
Pure selection for maximum production proved the winning long-run strategy, so indices weight yield alone.
Artificial insemination let one elite bull sire hundreds of thousands of daughters.
Genomic selection genotypes calves at birth and predicts lifetime performance, halving the generation interval.
config.correction: Pure production selection bred animals that grew brilliantly and fell apart reproductively; modern indices weight longevity, health and foot traits alongside yield.
config.why: The industry ran that experiment and paid for it in the 1990s. Low-heritability traits like fertility and disease resistance respond slowly, so they need deliberate selection pressure in a balanced index.

activities.caption: pair each mastitis control with what it attacks
activities.name: agMastitisMatch

config.prompt: Mastitis is the costliest dairy disease. Match each control to what it actually targets:

pairs.left: clean, dry teats and post-milking dips
pairs.right: contagious bacteria spreading cow-to-cow at milking
environmental bacteria picked up from the lying area
the herd's persistent reservoir of infection

pairs.left: somatic cell score on the national index
pairs.right: the heritable layer — breeding for resistance

config.why: Nearly every major livestock disease is a management-system disease first and an infection second: the vet treats the case, the husbandry treats the rate.

activities.caption: bet on the feed label question
activities.name: agGrainPredict

config.q: What is the honest nutritional comparison between grass-fed and grain-fed ruminant production?
choices: Grain-fed is simply better-fed, so it is always the higher standard
Grass is always superior, so grain feeding has no defensible role
Not grass vs grain, but what could this land grow otherwise — a systems question
The comparison is meaningless because both feeds have identical composition
config.why: Cattle cannot thrive on grain alone — rumen acidosis is the feedlot vet's daily case. Much ruminant production is valuable precisely because it runs on land and by-products unsuited to crops, so the question is a systems one, not a feed label.

activities.anchor: why farrowing rooms run heat lamps
activities.caption: which curve shows a cow's comfort zone?
activities.name: agComfortTrace

config.prompt: Performance against air temperature for a lactating dairy cow. Which shape shows a comfort zone sitting roughly between 5 and 20 °C, with yield falling away on both sides?

curves.label: a plateau around the mid-teens, falling away both sides
a peak up at newborn-piglet temperatures

config.why: A lactating cow's comfort zone is roughly 5–20 °C — she is a furnace shedding heat. Piglets sit at the other end, needing 30–34 °C at birth, which is why farrowing rooms heat the piglet, not the room.

activities.caption: pair each land-use principle with the economics behind it
activities.name: agLandEconMatch

config.prompt: The land-use principles are economic propositions in disguise. Match each to its economic form:

pairs.right: assigning the fixed input to its highest-valued use — opportunity cost
an investment decision — this year's lower margin buys next year's lower fertiliser bill
fertility as a depreciating asset unless replaced

config.why: Ricardo worked out land rent as a differential in 1815 and it still prices farmland: the same wheat price leaves a large surplus above costs on a fertile plain, barely covering them on thin upland soil — and that surplus is what a landowner can charge.

activities.caption: fill the gross margins and settle the comparison
activities.name: agGrossMarginCloze

config.text: Winter wheat: 8.5 t/ha at £180/t gives £1,530 of revenue; minus £620 of variable costs leaves a gross margin of £%%0%%/ha. Spring beans: 4.5 t/ha at £280/t gives £1,260 less £380, a gross margin of £%%1%%/ha. On paper wheat wins — but the beans fix nitrogen, cutting the wheat's fertiliser bill by perhaps £80/ha.
config.hint: Revenue minus variable costs, for each enterprise. Wheat: 1530 − 620. Beans: 1260 − 380.

activities.caption: guess the capital charge per hectare
activities.name: agCombineEstimate

config.prompt: A £150,000 combine is spread over 400 hectares. What is the capital charge per hectare?
config.why: £375/ha. Over 40 hectares the same machine would cost ten times that — £3,750/ha. Commodity gross margins are thin, so survival is a cost-position game, and that single arithmetic is the engine of two centuries of farm consolidation.
config.context: Ten times the cost per hectare on a farm a tenth the size — the whole consolidation story in one division.

activities.caption: file each move — commodity squeeze or escape route?
activities.name: agEscapeBuckets

config.prompt: A price-taker cannot charge more for a better job. File each strategy:

items.label: selling milling wheat at the market price
growing more hectares to spread fixed costs

config.why: Each escape substitutes a brand or a relationship for the anonymous commodity. But certification takes a three-year transition selling at conventional prices while managing lower yields — a capital investment in market position, not a free lunch.

activities.anchor: so over a decade the subsidy largely flows through into land prices
activities.caption: trace the subsidy past the cheque
activities.name: agSubsidyBranch

config.root: A government introduces a flat per-hectare direct payment decoupled from what is grown. A decade passes.

start.text: The payment is tied to land. What happens to the price anyone will pay for that land?

choices.label: Nothing — the money goes to whoever farms it
Land values and rents rise, absorbing much of the payment
choices.feedback: Capitalisation: the payment raises what anyone will bid for land.

nothing.text: Farms change hands at higher prices, and the new entrant's rent quietly absorbs the transfer. The cheque arrived; the margin did not.

capitalised.text: Over a decade the subsidy largely flows through into land prices and rents — benefiting landowners, who are not always the farmers. The transfer still worked, but not on the balance sheet people assumed.

config.why: Analysing a subsidy means tracing its effect through the channels it moves — what gets planted, how much fertiliser is applied, what land is worth — not reading the transfer cheque.

activities.anchor: price-inelastic (people and animals eat roughly the
activities.caption: which demand curve makes the cobweb explosive?
activities.name: agInelasticTrace

config.prompt: Demand for staple grains. Which curve shows the near-vertical, price-inelastic demand the cobweb model depends on — where a 12% supply rise needs a 40–60% price fall to clear?

curves.label: flat and elastic — small price moves shift a lot of volume
near-vertical — quantity barely moves however price swings

config.why: People and animals eat roughly the same amount whatever the price — short-run elasticity near −0.2. So supply surprises need violent price moves to clear, and the market traces a spider's web around equilibrium instead of settling on it.

activities.caption: true or false — the bumper harvest trap
activities.name: agCobwebJudge

statements.s: Supply decisions are made against last year's price but consumed at this year's price.
statements.why: A crop planted in spring cannot be un-planted in autumn — that lag is what makes the cobweb.

statements.s: A bumper harvest is always good news for farm incomes.
statements.why: With price-inelastic demand the extra supply needs a large price fall to clear, so revenue falls precisely when nature has been kindest.

statements.s: A harvest shortfall in one region can leave its farmers better off than a perfect season.
statements.why: The inverse of the bumper-harvest trap: less grain, higher price, inelastic demand.

statements.s: When the response over-corrects by more than the shock, the cycles widen.
statements.why: The explosive cobweb — elastic supply meeting inelastic demand — gave livestock farming its hog cycle, still visible in US hog prices.

activities.caption: guess the size of the transfer before it lands
activities.name: agSubsidyEstimate

config.prompt: Across the OECD's monitored countries, roughly how many billion US dollars per year were transferred to their agricultural sectors over 2021–23?
config.why: About 842 billion US dollars a year, the large majority flowing to individual producers through price supports, direct payments and subsidised insurance.
config.context: Close to a trillion dollars a year — the load-bearing policy behind the price-taker squeeze.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this budget
activities.name: agMarginSpot

config.prompt: A student reads the farm's accounts. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: The workhorse measure is gross margin: revenue per hectare minus variable costs per hectare.
Fixed costs — rent, machinery depreciation, buildings, insurance — are owed whether the crop succeeds or fails.
A gross margin of £900/ha therefore means the farm has made a profit of £900 on every hectare.
Profit subtracts the fixed costs too, and on most commodity farms fixed costs eat most of the gross margin.
A farm that knows its own total costs per tonne — and keeps them under the price — wins over a decade even through terrible years.
config.correction: A gross margin of £900/ha is not profit — fixed costs still have to come off it, and they usually eat most of it.
config.why: Gross margin is the first question (which enterprise to run) because fixed costs are nearly the same across alternatives. Profit is the second question, and it is a much harsher one.
